extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kantian aesthetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies Kantian criteria for aesthetic judgement and the beautiful (as explained in commentary/footnotes), including conditions for universal assent, disinterestedness, purposiveness, and distinctions among aesthetic kinds and artistic media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as the faculty of judging the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of taste is that it is the faculty of judging of the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of judgements of taste must show what is required to call an object beautiful; the aesthetical judgement first attends to the moment of quality. Taste is tied to a contemplative pleasure (passive satisfaction) rather than practical pleasure tied to desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement upon an object of satisfaction may be quite disinterested; judgements of taste do not in themselves establish any interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a judgement of taste to claim its special status it must be 'pure' — not based on a personal interest or a desire to possess the object. Disinterestedness means the satisfaction is not bound up with desire for the object's existence; social interest in having taste is a separate matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity requirement (not mingled with concepts or sensations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement must merely have reference to the relation of the cognitive powers put into activity to cognition in general and be pure, i.e. not mingled either with concepts of the Object or with sensations as determining grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a supposed aesthetic judgement is tainted by determinate concepts of the object or by sensation (e.g., private liking), then the claim to the special privilege (requesting universal assent) is an inaccurate application of the principle. Purity is necessary for the formal claim of universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for claiming universal assent of an aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be justified in claiming universal assent for an aesthetical judgement that rests merely on subjective grounds it is sufficient to assume (1) the subjective conditions of the Judgement ... are the same in all men, and (2) the judgement must merely have reference to this relation (consequently to the formal condition) and be pure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Communicability: the cognitive powers put into play must be common across persons; (2) Formality and purity: the judgement must concern the formal relation of faculties (not private interest or determinate concept), enabling a rightful demand for universal agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived purposiveness without an ascribable purpose indicates beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A flower (e.g. a tulip) is regarded as beautiful because in perceiving it we find a certain purposiveness which, in our judgement, is referred to no purpose at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When we perceive 'purposiveness' in an object but do not represent any definite purpose for it (as opposed to recognizing an artefact's function), there is immediate aesthetic satisfaction; by contrast, things we regard as works of art are often judged with reference to purpose and thus lack the same immediate aesthetic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular (typical) form vs characteristic exaggeration (caricature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfectly regular countenance ordinarily tells us nothing because it contains nothing characteristic and rather expresses the Idea of the race than the specific traits of a person; the exaggeration of a characteristic that does violence to the normal Idea is called caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey individuality, some departure from mere regularity (i.e., the addition or exaggeration of distinguishing features) is necessary; an entirely symmetric or idealized face tends to indicate mediocrity and lacks expressive specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between affections and passions (aesthetic consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affections are specifically different from passions. The former are related merely to feeling; the latter belong to the faculty of desire. Affections are stormy and unpremeditated; passions are steady and deliberate. The latter can never be called sublime because in a passion the freedom of the mind is abolished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the experience of the sublime, one must avoid responses that amount to passions (which override freedom); the sublime is compatible with affective, non-deliberative states that do not eliminate moral freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as contemplative (passive) satisfaction versus practical pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure which is not necessarily bound up with the desire of the object ... may be called mere contemplative pleasure or passive satisfaction. The feeling of the latter kind of pleasure we call taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish aesthetic pleasure (taste) from practical pleasure that serves desire or use; aesthetic evaluation attends to pleasure that clings to representation alone rather than to possession or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of taste in arts of speech should be in dead/learned languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of taste as regards the arts of speech must be composed in a dead and learned language. The first [reason] is that they may not suffer that change which inevitably comes over living languages; the second, because learned languages have a grammar which is subject to no wanton change of fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When establishing canonical exemplars for rhetorical or literary taste, prefer stable, classical linguistic exemplars so that rules and noble expressions remain constant rather than fashionable and transient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of the arts by expression of aesthetical Ideas and freedom of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to combine the beautiful arts under one principle, viz. that of the expression of aesthetical Ideas (according to the analogy of speech). Landscape gardening may be regarded as a species of the art of painting when it takes forms from nature and involves merely the free play of the Imagination in contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group or judge arts by whether they express aesthetical Ideas and invoke free imaginative contemplation (as in painting and certain forms of landscaping) vs arts conditioned by definite concepts or purposes (as in architecture). This is offered as a non-definitive scheme, one of several possible attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conversational structure: narrative → discussion → jest
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant was accustomed to say that the talk at a dinner table should always pass through these three stages — narrative, discussion, and jest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pleasing social discourse (and practical deployment of wit/humor), structure exchanges by first telling stories (narrative), then engaging in reflective exchange (discussion), and finishing with light, jocular remarks (jest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between art as craft and art as display/performative mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Common people may say 'that is not art, it is only science' when the how is known; they call the display (e.g., rope-dancer) 'art'. If we know how, we can do it; rope-dancer's performance earns the term 'art'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing whether something is 'art', consider whether it is judged for skillful performance/display (performative art) rather than mere technical know-how; the social ascription of 'art' often attaches to feats of performance rather than mechanical reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric (readiness and accuracy) belongs to beautiful art but manipulative oratory is dishonourable
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness and accuracy in speaking (which taken together constitute Rhetoric) belong to beautiful art; but the art of the orator, the art of availing oneself of the weaknesses of men for one's own designs, is worthy of no respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value rhetorical skill when it serves truthful, morally sympathetic communication (the ideal 'vir bonus discendi peritus'); condemn rhetorical art aimed at manipulation even if it is effective.
